analysis.one_liner: Lets the Wards Cove salmon cannery workers sue under the new civil rights law's rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate labor committee approved the bill in March 1992, but it never came to a floor vote before Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1989 the Supreme Court ruled in Wards Cove Packing Co. v. Antonio that workers suing over hiring practices with discriminatory effects must prove the employer had no business justification. When Congress wrote the Civil Rights Act of 1991 to restore the easier, pre-1989 rules, negotiators carved out one exception: the Wards Cove cannery workers themselves, whose case was already in court, were excluded. This bill would have deleted that carve-out, so the workers' pending case could be judged under the new, fairer burden-of-proof rules.
analysis.who_benefits: The mostly Filipino American and Alaska Native salmon cannery workers who sued Wards Cove Packing Co., plus future plaintiffs with older pending cases, who would have been able to use the new law's rules placing the burden of justifying discriminatory practices on the employer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wards Cove cannery workers suing their employer

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the exclusion in the Civil Rights Act of 1991 for disparate impact cases filed before March 1, 1975 and decided after October 30, 1983 — the category covering the Wards Cove case [S2] [S3].
Restores the burden-shifting rule from Wards Cove Packing Co. v. Antonio, under which employers, not workers, must justify a practice with discriminatory effects [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Wards Cove Packing Co. and other employers with long-pending discrimination cases, who would face the new law's easier-to-satisfy plaintiffs and potential back pay liability in cases already underway.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with old pending discrimination suits

drawbacks.text: It changes the legal rules for a lawsuit already in progress, which raises the ordinary fairness objection to retroactive application of new law to pending cases [S2] [S3].
The exclusion it targets was a negotiated compromise that helped win enactment of the broader Civil Rights Act of 1991; reopening it risked unsettling that settlement of a contentious fight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a narrow, specific unfairness: one group of workers was written out of a civil rights law whose rules would otherwise have applied to their pending case. The cost falls on a single company and a small set of employers with old cases, and the main counterargument is the general one against changing rules mid-litigation. For the workers involved, the stakes were their entire discrimination claim.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved it in March 1992, but no senator ever got to vote on it on the floor before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Brock Adams introduced the bill on November 13, 1991, drafted to amend the Civil Rights Act of 1991 'if enacted' — the 1991 law was still pending final enactment at the time [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on November 13, 1991 [S1].
On March 11, 1992, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment [S1].
The bill never received a Senate floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wards Cove Packing Co. and the employers the exclusion shielded were better off: the carve-out stayed in the Civil Rights Act of 1991, and the cannery workers never gained the new law's rules for their case.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wards Cove Packing and protected employers

for.name: Sen. Brock Adams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strike the Wards Cove exclusion from the Civil Rights Act of 1991.

for.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Approved the bill in markup on March 11, 1992, ordering it reported favorably without amendment.

for.name: Sens. Paul Simon, Daniel Akaka, Daniel Inouye, and Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Joined Adams in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

against.name: George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Signed the Civil Rights Act of 1991 only after negotiators included the Wards Cove exclusion he had sought, which this bill would have undone.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it cleared committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsor appears in the record; the exclusion the bill targeted was the compromise that won a Republican president's signature on the 1991 civil rights law [S4].

industries.industry: Seafood processing and cannery operators (Wards Cove Packing Co.)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the carve-out that kept the workers' suit under the old rules, making it easier for them to win and exposing the company to liability.
The 1991 Act's exclusion let older cases be decided under rules friendlier to employers; this bill would have removed that protection for the covered cases.
